Lessons.Title: Points, Lines, Rays, and Segments
ExplanationParagraphs: 2021 Grade 4 Unit 7 Lesson 2 formalizes points, lines, rays and segments after the exploratory descriptions of Lesson 1. A point is a location (the drawn dot is only its marker); a straight line extends in two directions, a ray has one endpoint and extends one direction, and a segment has two endpoints.

Number Talk (10 minutes): mentally evaluate the source expressions 90 − 45 = 45, 270 − 45 = 225, 270 − 135 = 135, 360 − 135 = 225; compare adjustment and place-value subtraction strategies without substituting this warm-up for the geometry goal.

Card Sort (20 minutes): in groups of 2–4, sort original illustrated or descriptive point, line, ray and segment cards into four categories. Discuss the no-size property of a geometric point, why complete lines are unmeasurable, how rays have one end, and why segments have two. Teacher checks physical figures and spoken justifications.

Dot-field drawing (15 minutes): use a ruler to make a triangle, rhombus, trapezoid, hexagon, pentagon and rectangle from line segments; then use a combination of rays and segments to form an uppercase letter, numeral and lowercase letter. Endpoints can be points even without a printed dot.

Synthesis (10 minutes): compare original student constructions, clarify rays versus segments and the infinite line, then have students add geometric diagrams and meanings to an individual word wall. First-party Cool-down: draw ray PQ and segment PQ and explain which mark continues beyond Q; not the publisher-protected assessment.

Digital Practice combines independently authored geometric description-classification cards with the four original numerical Number Talk expressions. It does not grade the source publisher's card sorting, student figure drawings or oral comparison.

KeyConcepts.Title: Point and line
KeyConcepts.Definition: A point is a location, and a line is a straight path that continues indefinitely in both directions.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A drawn dot symbolizes a point but its marker size is not a property of the point. A line has no endpoints.
KeyConcepts.Example: A line through points A and B has straight continuation beyond both A and B.

KeyConcepts.Title: Ray
KeyConcepts.Definition: A ray is a straight part of a line with one endpoint and continuation in one direction.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A ray named PQ starts at P and continues through Q; reversing its order changes its starting point.
KeyConcepts.Example: Ray PQ starts at P, passes Q and goes on beyond Q.

KeyConcepts.Title: Line segment
KeyConcepts.Definition: A line segment is the finite straight part between two endpoints.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Segment PQ has endpoints P and Q and does not continue past either.
KeyConcepts.Example: A triangle has three line-segment sides that meet at its corner points.

WorkedExamples.Title: Mental Number Talk: related differences
WorkedExamples.Question: Calculate mentally 90−45, 270−45, 270−135 and 360−135.
WorkedExamples.Method: Compensate or split hundreds/tens; check each by addition.
Steps: 90−45=45 and 270−45=225: increase the minuend by 180, so the difference also increases by 180.

WorkedExamples.Title: Sort four geometry descriptions
WorkedExamples.Question: A card has a single dot; another describes a straight path with arrows both ways; a third has one endpoint and one arrow; a fourth has two endpoints. Sort them.
WorkedExamples.Method: Count endpoints, note direction of extension, and distinguish a location from a straight figure.
Steps: A dot that names only one location represents a point.
A straight line continuing both directions is a line; one endpoint and one-direction extension represents a ray.
The finite straight figure between two endpoints is a line segment.
WorkedExamples.Check: Point has no intrinsic size; line has zero endpoints; ray one; segment two.

WorkedExamples.Title: Dot-paper constructions
WorkedExamples.Question: On a dot field, construct a triangle, rhombus, trapezoid, hexagon, pentagon and rectangle using segments. Then make three characters using rays and segments.
WorkedExamples.Method: Connect chosen points with the required straight pieces and show ray continuations.
Steps: For each polygon trace straight segments joining vertices; use three for a triangle, five for a pentagon and six for a hexagon.
Check the other requested polygons by their side/parallel attributes: rhombus and rectangle have four sides; a trapezoid has a parallel pair under the curriculum's convention.
Make one uppercase letter, numeral and lowercase letter; use arrows to distinguish any rays from finite segments, and explain whether endpoints are marked.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Valid drawings and clear explanations, teacher-reviewed against dot field and original task.
WorkedExamples.Check: The teacher checks geometric validity and group explanations, not merely the number of edges.

WorkedExamples.Title: First-party Cool-down: ray and segment PQ
WorkedExamples.Question: Draw a ray from P passing through Q and the segment joining P and Q. Which figure continues beyond Q?
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare which ends carry an endpoint or arrow.
Steps: Label two distinct points P and Q.
Draw segment PQ ending at both labelled points.
Draw ray PQ starting at P and passing Q, extending beyond Q; explain the arrow.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Ray PQ continues beyond Q; segment PQ stops at Q. Teacher reviews the actual drawing.
WorkedExamples.Check: An original Edulytics task, not the inaccessible publisher Cool-down.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Saying a mathematical point has the size of its dot.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A drawn dot is only a visible mark; the geometric point marks a location without size.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use a dot to represent a location; do not give the point a measurable length or area.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Drawing a ray with arrows on both ends or a segment with an arrow.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A ray has one endpoint and continues one direction; a line continues both ways; a segment stops at both ends.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare the number and location of endpoints and arrowheads on each drawing.

SummaryPoints: Point = location; line = straight and extends both ways; ray = one endpoint; segment = two endpoints.
Teacher sorts source four-category cards, then reviews six requested polygons and three characters made using dots/rays/segments.
Edulytics first-party Cool-down and online description classification do not certify publisher figure parity.
